I decided to build a full-stack WhatsApp alternative completely from scratch — sub-50ms latency, zero Firebase, and verified cross-platform parity on Apple iOS and Google Android. ⚡

During my Mobile Application Development (HHDP 1) module, I built Tappsy: pairing the proven UX patterns of WhatsApp (Chats/Updates/Calls tabs, speech bubbles with directional tails, double blue ticks ✓✓, status story rings) with an electric brand identity (#0084FF).

💡 Key Engineering Highlights:
• Instant Sub-50ms Messaging: Bidirectional WebSockets (wss://) hosted on a native Java EE / Jakarta EE server (@ServerEndpoint), eliminating polling overhead and conserving mobile battery life.
• Resilient Socket Engine: Custom client-side heartbeat loop (Ping/Pong) with exponential backoff to handle mobile network handovers cleanly.
• Dual-Theme Parity: Complete Light (#FFFFFF) and Dark Mode (#0F172A Slate) styling dynamically syncing with system appearance via custom ThemeProvider & NativeWind.
• End-to-End Onboarding: Animated flow with country-code dialing (+94 Sri Lanka defaults), SHA-256 PIN security, and multipart avatar uploads.
• Dual-Platform Verification: Captured live on both Apple iOS Simulator (iPhone 18 Pro) and Google Android Emulator (Pixel 9a).

One of the fastest ways to trigger a React hydration mismatch in a Next.js App Router application is a single line of date formatting code.

Everything looks completely normal on your local machine. Then you deploy to production, and the browser console throws a hydration error while dates briefly flicker on mobile screens.

Here is why it happens:
Your Next.js Server Component renders the HTML on a Vercel server running in UTC time. When the user opens the page in Jakarta, Sydney, or London, their browser runs client-side hydration using their local timezone and locale settings.

If your component calls new Date().toLocaleDateString() directly during render, the server output and the browser output do not match. React rejects the mismatch and forces an expensive client re-render.

Here are three clean ways we eliminate timezone hydration bugs in production:

1. Lock the Timezone Explicitly on Both Sides:
Never rely on implicit default locales inside Intl.DateTimeFormat or toLocaleDateString. Pass both the locale and an explicit timeZone parameter (for example, 'en-US' and 'UTC' or a stored user timezone preference from the database) so the server and browser produce the exact same string.

2. Defer Local User Timezone Formatting Until Mount:
If you genuinely need the visitor's local browser clock (like "2 hours ago" or local event times), render a deterministic fallback or ISO date on the server, then update to the local string inside a small isolated client wrapper after mount. Never wrap an entire page in a mounted check just to format a timestamp.

3. Pass Serialized ISO Strings Across Server-Client Boundaries:
Pass plain ISO strings from Server Components into Client Components instead of raw Date instances or pre-formatted strings that drop timezone offsets.

Hydration bugs rarely come from complicated business logic. Nine times out of ten, they come from small assumptions about browser globals like window, Date, or invalid nested HTML tags.

The US spent months figuring out how to keep China away from American chips. Chinese labs, meanwhile, just asked ChatGPT and trained on its answers. OpenAI's rules forbid this; the law doesn't.

On November 16, the US Commerce Department closed an old loophole. Chinese companies have long been banned from buying advanced Nvidia chips, but could rent them in a data center in Singapore or Malaysia and work remotely. Now any data center anywhere that leases Chinese customers a lot of that compute needs a US license — for the law, renting is now the same as exporting. Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, and Brazil now need Washington's permission just to buy these chips at all.

The trigger was the Nvidia scandal: Singapore's Megaspeed bought about $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over three years, and investigators believe it used shell companies to grant access to 240,000 chips banned from export to China. The company denies everything. The affair ended with Jensen Huang's resignation. A similar rule had been blocked by Commerce Secretary Lutnick back in summer 2025, and was only adopted after the resignation.

That same day, Reuters published an investigation based on more than 300 Chinese papers, patents, and job listings. The conclusion: in China it's become standard practice to take American models' answers and train on them — "distillation" — with dedicated software and hired staff now built around it. A Shanghai university turned about 5,000 OpenAI model answers into training data for an Alibaba model. Alibaba itself has described generating data via GPT-4. Meituan, the Chinese food-delivery service, trained its models on GPT-4o. In January, eight Chinese ministries issued a state program explicitly backing distillation as a way to cut AI costs.

A US official told Reuters that Washington sees this as the main reason Chinese models have nearly caught up with American ones. People familiar with Chinese developers' work disagree, calling it one factor among many, alongside engineering and data. Anthropic says it recently learned to block most such attempts.

One more detail: the same rule also scrapped the Biden-era export controls on trained models themselves. Chips are now guarded by licenses worldwide, but their output is still freely available through any chat window.

For the average user, the takeaway is simple: cheap Chinese models that are "almost like Claude at a third of the price" are partly cheap because they trained on American answers. The investigation's examples span 2024–2026 models, and the rental rule is still temporary — it's open for public comment for another 60 days.

TRUMP × XI: Five countries, 90 days & a new front in the AI race.

Who bears the economic cost?

On 16 November 2026, ahead of Trump's scheduled 19 November meeting with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, Washington tightened controls on advanced US AI computing.

According to the US Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), the rule targets not only physical chip exports but remote access to computing power through overseas data centres. It introduces additional licensing for covered advanced chips destined for Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia and Brazil. Certain existing data centres supplying significant compute to restricted-country firms have 90 days from the rule's effective date to secure licences.

The regulation also identifies a threshold of 12 million Total Processing Performance (TPP) for covered computing arrangements. This is a technical regulatory measure—not a dollar value or a forecast of losses.

The consequences differ by industry in my humble opinion:

For Nvidia and US chipmakers, restrictions can protect a national-security advantage but also limit access to Chinese-linked demand. Lost sales are only part of the equation: fewer customers using American hardware could eventually weaken the surrounding software ecosystem.

For Chinese AI developers, renting computing capacity abroad becomes harder. Domestic alternatives may gain investment, although replacing Nvidia also requires advanced memory, packaging, software and energy-efficient performance.

For Southeast Asian data centres, licensing uncertainty could change projected utilisation and financing terms. That can reach construction firms, electricity suppliers and grid investors, even before a project is cancelled. 

Crucially, the five countries face licensing requirements, not a blanket chip ban.

For Europe, the warning is structural: industrial AI increasingly depends on chips and cloud capacity governed by decisions outside Europe. Building alternatives could improve resilience, but at considerable cost.

My assessment: Washington is extending control from the sale of chips to access to the computing capacity they provide. That may slow China's frontier-AI development. Yet if restrictions accelerate viable Chinese substitutes and make third-country investors diversify away from US technology, America's long-term leverage could erode.

Xi faces the opposite dilemma: pay the cost of dependence now or the cost of technological substitution over years.

The test is not how many restrictions Washington announces, but how many licences it denies, which investments shift, and whether China's alternatives actually close the performance gap.

Controlling access is not the same as sustaining leadership.

Financing the organization that develops infrastructure is not the same as financing the infrastructure itself.

Four complementary forms of capital matter:

1. Corporate and development finance funds engineering, permitting, feedstock security and commercial preparation to bring projects toward investment readiness.

2. Project finance funds individual assets, with debt service supported by project cash flows and contractual commitments.

Three things worth knowing today, and all three point at the same gap: nobody has agreed on how to verify any of this.

1. The US closed the remote-access loophole. Yesterday, Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim final rule requiring licences to export, re-export or transfer advanced AI chips to Brazil, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand, and obliging data centres and exporters to run due diligence on who ultimately owns the customer. The stated target: Chinese developers renting American compute from third countries. Compute is now a jurisdiction question, not a procurement one.

2. The Fed put a shape on the downside. Chair Kevin Warsh told a San Francisco task force that AI "will have significant impact on the economy," then named a third scenario: if expected returns turn down and equity valuations fall, you get a slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment. Recovery, but without the productivity. That is a central bank treating AI capex as a macro variable.

3. Medical AI got graded, and the grades are low. InclusionMed, released this week, scored 22 frontier models across five audited benchmarks. The index range: 17.5 to 49.1 out of 100. No model cleared 50. Every model in the top ten scored higher on patient communication than on clinical decision-making. And of 1,034 tagged tasks, only 338 had a determinable geography - 318 of those American.

Read together, the binding constraint is verification. Can you prove where the compute runs, whether the return arrives, and whether the model is actually right?

So the question I would put to you: what is the one number your AI programme is judged on this quarter - and who outside your own team can check it?

Norway just agreed to buy almost 21 million tonnes of carbon cuts. It pays on delivery.

On Monday, Norway signed two 10 year deals under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement: up to 8.78 million tonnes of carbon credits from Morocco, and up to 12 million tonnes of emission reductions from Indonesia. The money supports new renewable projects in both countries. The price was not disclosed. Of course it was not.

The clause I would frame: Norway pays only after the reductions are achieved, verified and delivered.

That sounds obvious. It is not how a lot of this market has worked. Buyers have prepaid for promises, then spent years chasing the tonnes.

Same weekend, at COP31 in Antalya, dozens of countries asked for the UN's new carbon market to reassess its integrity rules, after an industry push. One camp says make the rules easier. Norway says fine, but I pay when it shows up.

I have spent years designing carbon methodologies and registries. Pay on delivery is not a lack of trust. Nobody in Quebec prepays for maple syrup from trees that have not been tapped.

Pay on delivery is a methodology too.

Buyers and developers: is pay on delivery fair to projects that need money upfront, or is it the only deal that should exist?

U.S. export controls now reach rented AI computing power
- Washington is tightening its grip on how Chinese companies access advanced American chips, including those they never physically import.
- Rules announced by the Commerce Department on 16 November target a route around existing restrictions: renting computing power from overseas data centers to train AI models.
- The mechanism centers on hardware exports. Certain advanced chips and servers supplied to overseas data centers will require licenses if those facilities provide substantial computing to companies headquartered in China or other restricted countries. The requirement also covers companies whose ultimate parent is based there.
- The rule takes effect on 19 November. Operators already serving affected customers have 90 days to obtain authorization or risk future export restrictions. Applications will be assessed case by case.
- Advanced chip shipments to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, and Brazil will also require licenses because Commerce considers them potential diversion routes. Qualifying U.S.-headquartered end users are exempt but must submit reports.
- For data center operators, the commercial implications are substantial:
Customer ownership and ultimate parent companies become central to access to American hardware.
- Contracts with Chinese AI developers face greater regulatory uncertainty.
Chip exporters and foreign foundries face closer scrutiny of their customers.
- The broader shift is clear: Washington is extending controls from where chips are shipped to who benefits from their computing power.
- The *enforcement challenge* is *identifying* the *ultimate customer*. A data center may contract with a locally registered company while the computing serves a Chinese parent or client.
- The likely result is a continuing contest between tighter customer checks and attempts to secure access through intermediaries. How effectively operators establish ownership and end use will help determine whether these rules materially slow Chinese AI development. #Geopolitics #AI #Compute #Chips

Responsible Scale #09 | Capital Is Not the Problem. Bankability Is.

The world is not short of capital. It is short of infrastructure projects that capital can confidently finance.

ASEAN’s challenge is not simply attracting billions. It is building the industrial foundations that make those billions investable.

In Responsible Scale #08, I explored why ASEAN needs integrated energy infrastructure. Now comes the harder question: how do we turn industrial ambition into bankable projects?

Financing the organization that develops infrastructure is not the same as financing the infrastructure itself.

Four complementary forms of capital matter:

1. Corporate and development finance funds engineering, permitting, feedstock security and commercial preparation to bring projects toward investment readiness.

2. Project finance funds individual assets, with debt service supported by project cash flows and contractual commitments.

3. Infrastructure funds and sovereign wealth funds can provide long-term equity at corporate, platform or project level, according to mandate and maturity.

4. Green bonds can finance eligible investments with defined uses of proceeds, governance and transparent reporting. Green credentials cannot replace sound economics.

Capital does not make infrastructure bankable. Bankable projects attract capital.

Cargo first. Port second. Capital follows bankability.

A deep-sea port without credible cargo demand carries substantial risk. Integrated with processing plants, refineries and energy infrastructure, it serves identifiable feedstock flows, exports and logistics needs.

This is the logic behind TARMO’s Steung Hav gateway in Cambodia: develop the industrial ecosystem that generates cargo demand, rather than build a port and wait for industry.

Design for scale. Finance in phases.

TARMO’s integrated vertical value chain connects upstream operations in India, Cambodia and Indonesia with downstream industrial, energy and maritime infrastructure in Cambodia.
Early operations are designed to generate cash flows that progressively de-risk subsequent investments. Modular engineering allows capacity and capital deployment to follow verified demand and operating performance.

Integrated by design. Modular in execution. Scalable by demand.

Our independent dMRV platform is designed to support financial monitoring, cash-flow transparency, operational traceability and measurable environmental performance.

Our philosophy: finance the development platform, then structure each asset around its readiness, revenues and risks.

The future belongs not to those who announce the largest investments, but to those who engineer bankability—and deliver at scale.

Would you let strangers on the internet redesign part of a jet engine?

In 2013 General Electric, one of the world's biggest makers of jet engines, did exactly that. The part was a metal bracket that crews use to move an engine weighing nearly six tonnes, which is not the kind of thing most companies hand to the public. Anyone could enter, and nearly 700 people from 56 countries did. The company hoped for a part 30% lighter. The winner, an engineer in Salatiga, Indonesia, cut its weight by 84%. His bracket weighed less than a can of drink, and in testing it held about four tonnes.

Inside most organisations, "let anyone design it" doesn't get that far. Someone suggests it, there's a short laugh, and the meeting moves back to the plan everyone expected. Nobody decided the idea was bad. It just never got a second minute.

Next time an idea sounds unrealistic, give it that minute before anyone judges it. Ask what the person is hoping for, then look for a version that could work. GE didn't hand over a whole engine. It handed over one bracket, and 3D printed and load-tested the top ten designs before trusting any of them.

posts.text:
Your CV has about 10 seconds. Here’s how to make them count.

I’ve spent 12 years across brand, eCommerce, and digital marketing, and I’ve seen so many CVs as part of the job: hiring manager for several roles. Here’s what I’ve learned, using the Harvard CV format as the base:

1. Compact pages, reverse chronological, no fluff.
Harvard’s format is simple on purpose: Education, Experience, Leadership & Activities, Skills. No objective statement, no “I am a hardworking team player,” no graphics, no skill bars.

2. Every bullet = action + scope + result.
Before: “Responsible for managing marketing campaigns.”
After: “Led 12 integrated campaigns across 4 channels, increasing repeat purchase rate by 18% in 6 months.”
Same job, completely different signal. (Use your real numbers. If you don’t have a number, show scale: budget, team size, audience, or frequency.)

3. Photo or no photo?
My honest take: skip it. For multinational, tech, and startup roles, a photo adds nothing and can invite bias. It can also break ATS parsing. The exception is some local companies and industries in Indonesia that still expect one. Check the company’s culture and the job posting first, don’t assume.

4. Make it skimmable.
Consistent fonts, consistent date formats, and 3 to 5 bullets per role. Your most recent roles get the most space, and old ones shrink.

5. Tailor it, always.
Mirror the language of the job description where it’s true. One generic CV sent to 50 jobs loses to one sharp CV sent to 5.

A good CV doesn’t list everything you’ve done. It makes the reader’s decision easy.

What’s the one thing on your CV you’re unsure about? Drop it in the comments.

-   Conduct retest to verify fix effectiveness and ensure long-term risk mitigation
-   Drive continuous improvement by building internal tooling, refining checklist/playbook and mentoring junior team member
 
 
Requirement:
-   Minimum 4 years of experience in offensive security or 7 years in general cybersecurity with at least 4 years exclusively focus on penetration testing, experience bug bounty.
